relevance_reason: Identifies HPSE2 mutations as the cause of urofacial syndrome, maps the locus to 10q23-q24, and gives evidence of genetic heterogeneity.

findings.statement: Daly et al. (2010) described urofacial syndrome (UFS) as a rare autosomal recessive disease characterized by facial grimacing when attempting to smile and failure of the urinary bladder to void completely despite a lack of anatomical bladder outflow obstruction or overt neurological damage. They noted that UFS individuals often have reflux of infected urine from the bladder to the upper renal tract, with a risk of kidney damage and renal failure.
quotes: Urofacial syndrome (UFS) is a rare autosomal recessive disease characterized by facial grimacing when attempting to smile and failure of the urinary bladder to void completely despite a lack of anatomical bladder outflow obstruction or overt neurological damage.
UFS individuals often have reflux of infected urine from the bladder to the upper renal tract, with a risk of kidney damage and renal failure.

phenotypes.text: facial grimacing when attempting to smile

findings.statement: By whole-genome SNP mapping in one affected individual, Daly et al. (2010) defined an autozygous region of 16 Mb on chromosome 10q23-q24.
quotes: Whole-genome SNP mapping in one affected individual defined an autozygous region of 16 Mb on chromosome 10q23-q24, within which a 10 kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of HPSE2 was identified.

findings.statement: Within the 10q23-q24 autozygous region, Daly et al. (2010) identified a 10-kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of the HPSE2 gene in an individual with urofacial syndrome.
quotes: Whole-genome SNP mapping in one affected individual defined an autozygous region of 16 Mb on chromosome 10q23-q24, within which a 10 kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of HPSE2 was identified.

variants.as_reported: 10 kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of HPSE2

findings.statement: Daly et al. (2010) identified homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in the HPSE2 gene in 5 further unrelated families with urofacial syndrome, confirming HPSE2 as the causative gene.
quotes: Homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in five further unrelated families confirmed HPSE2 as the causative gene for UFS.

findings.statement: Daly et al. (2010) did not identify HPSE2 mutations in 4 additional patients with urofacial syndrome, which they concluded indicated genetic heterogeneity.
quotes: Mutations were not identified in four additional UFS patients, indicating genetic heterogeneity.

findings.statement: Daly et al. (2010) showed that HPSE2 is expressed in the fetal and adult central nervous system, where they suggested it might be involved in controlling facial expression and urinary voiding. It is also expressed in bladder smooth muscle, which they considered consistent with a role in renal tract morphology and function.
quotes: We show that HPSE2 is expressed in the fetal and adult central nervous system, where it might be implicated in controlling facial expression and urinary voiding, and also in bladder smooth muscle, consistent with a role in renal tract morphology and function.

relevance_reason: Identifies loss-of-function mutations in HPSE2 as the cause of autosomal recessive urofacial syndrome.

findings.statement: Pang et al. (2010) identified loss-of-function mutations in the HPSE2 gene in all patients with urofacial syndrome they studied, who came from Colombia, the United States, and France. HPSE2 lies in the chromosome 10q24 region that the authors had previously found by homozygosity mapping.
quotes: Mutations with a loss of function in the Heparanase 2 (HPSE2) gene were identified in all UFS patients originating from Colombia, the United States, and France.
Previously, we localized the defective gene for the urofacial syndrome (UFS) to a region on chromosome 10q24 by homozygosity mapping.

findings.statement: Pang et al. (2010) suggested that because UFS patients completely lack HPSE2 function, HPSE2 may be important for the coordinated action of the muscles used in facial expression and urine voiding.
quotes: Complete loss of HPSE2 function in UFS patients suggests that HPSE2 may be important for the synergic action of muscles implicated in facial expression and urine voiding.

findings.statement: Pang et al. (2010) noted that they had previously mapped the urofacial syndrome gene to chromosome 10q24 by homozygosity mapping.
quotes: Previously, we localized the defective gene for the urofacial syndrome (UFS) to a region on chromosome 10q24 by homozygosity mapping.

relevance_reason: A case report of a Turkish patient with urofacial syndrome; it adds clinical evidence but no molecular data.

findings.statement: Derbent et al. (2009) reported a patient from Turkey with urofacial syndrome. The authors described it as the first published case of the syndrome in that country. The patient had been followed for recurrent urinary tract infection and vesicoureteral reflux and was not diagnosed until age 16 years. The authors stressed that recognizing the characteristic facial grimacing allows early diagnosis, which matters for managing the urinary problems.
quotes: We report the first published case of urofacial syndrome in Turkey. The patient was diagnosed at 16 years of age, after having been followed with the diagnosis of recurrent urinary tract infection and vesico-ureteral reflux.

findings.statement: Derbent et al. (2009) described urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome as a rare autosomal recessive disorder. Patients have an 'inverted' facial expression, so that they appear to be crying when they smile. They also have serious urinary tract problems, including enuresis, urinary tract infection and hydronephrosis. Some severely affected patients become hypertensive and progress to end-stage renal disease.
quotes: Urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome is a rare autosomal-recessive disorder that features an unusual "inverted" facial expression, such that patients appear to be crying when they smile.
The urinary issues usually result in enuresis, urinary tract infection, and hydronephrosis, and some severely affected patients become hypertensive and progress to end-stage renal disease.

relevance_reason: Abstract reports a case series of 11 Turkish patients with urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome from five families; it adds clinical cases but no molecular data.

findings.statement: Aydogdu et al. (2010) reported 11 patients with urofacial syndrome from 5 families from Turkey, followed for a median of 32 months (range, 2 to 44 months). The authors described the syndrome as having uropathy and facial abnormalities, and stressed that early diagnosis is crucial for managing urinary problems caused by a dysfunctional bladder.
quotes: We report 11 patients with urofacial syndrome in five families from Turkey with a median follow up of 32 months (range, 2-44 months).
characterized by uropathy and facial abnormalities. Early diagnosis is crucial for the management and prognosis of urinary problems due to a dysfunctional bladder.

findings.statement: Aydogdu et al. (2010) described urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome as a rare autosomal recessive condition that occurs in both sexes.
quotes: The urofacial syndrome, also known as Ochoa syndrome, is a rare autosomal recessive condition that occurs in both genders

relevance_reason: Refines the UFS critical region on 10q23-q24 and excludes candidate genes (ACDP1, GOT1). Also gives evidence that a single locus underlies UFS across ethnic groups.

findings.statement: Wang et al. (2003) built a genomic sequence map covering the urofacial syndrome interval on chromosome 10q23-q24, which had earlier been placed in a region of about 360 kb by homozygosity mapping. They narrowed the critical region to 220 kb. This region contains the newly identified ACDP1 gene and part of the GOT1 gene, which had already been excluded as a UFS candidate.
quotes: we have constructed a genomic sequence map covering the entire UFS interval and narrowed the disease interval to a genomic region of 220 kb that harbor the newly identified ACDP1 gene in addition to part of the GOT1 gene which has already been excluded as a candidate for UFS

findings.statement: Wang et al. (2003) searched ACDP1 extensively in UFS patients, including the coding region, the 5-prime and 3-prime untranslated regions, the promoter, and the exon/intron junctions. They found no pathogenic mutation.
quotes: Extensive search for mutations in the coding region, the 5' and 3' untranslated regions, the promoter region, and the exon/intron junctions failed to identify a pathogenic mutation in UFS patients.

findings.statement: From their analyses, Wang et al. (2003) concluded that the same chromosome 10q gene causes UFS in all patients, across multiple ethnic groups.
quotes: our analyses indicated that the same gene on chromosome 10q is responsible for all UFS patients from multiple ethnic groups

findings.statement: Wang et al. (2003) described urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome as a rare disorder with congenital obstructive uropathy and abnormal facial expression, caused by a single recessive gene.
quotes: The urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome (UFS) characterized by congenital obstructive uropathy and abnormal facial expression is a rare disorder caused by a single recessive disease gene.

relevance_reason: This is a case report of three European patients with urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome. It adds cases from outside Colombia, but only the abstract is available, and it gives few details.

findings.statement: Garcia-Minaur et al. (2001) reported 3 European patients with urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome, a disorder originally described in Colombian patients. They suggested that the syndrome may be missed because the urinary problems vary and the characteristic facial grimacing is not recognized.
quotes: We report on three European cases of urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome.
It is likely that they may be missed because of variability of the urinary problems and failure to recognize the characteristic facial grimacing.

findings.statement: Garcia-Minaur et al. (2001) stressed that an early diagnosis of urofacial syndrome has important consequences for managing the urinary problems and for their prognosis.
quotes: Establishing an early diagnosis has important consequences for the management and prognosis of urinary problems in these patients.

relevance_reason: Reports the first European (French) family with urofacial syndrome and haplotype analysis consistent with linkage to 10q23-q24, supporting genetic homogeneity.

findings.statement: Chauve et al. (2000) reported the first European cases of urofacial syndrome, in a French family. Haplotype analysis in this family, compared with previously reported haplotypes in Colombian and American patients, was compatible with localization of the critical region to chromosome 10q23-q24.
quotes: We report the first European cases of UFS.

Haplotype analyses in our French family were compared with those previously described in patients from Columbia and America (literature data). The results are compatible with the same localization of the critical region

findings.statement: Chauve et al. (2000) concluded that the haplotype results in a French family favored the hypothesis of genetic homogeneity of urofacial syndrome.
quotes: The results are compatible with the same localization of the critical region and favor the hypothesis of genetic homogeneity.

relevance_reason: Mapping refinement, genetic homogeneity, and candidate gene exclusion for urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome.

findings.statement: Wang et al. (1999) used homozygosity mapping in American patients of Irish heritage to show that urofacial syndrome in these patients mapped to the same 10q23-q24 region previously identified in families from Colombia. They concluded that the syndrome is genetically homogeneous.
quotes: Here we demonstrate genetic homogeneity of the syndrome through homozygosity mapping in American patients with Irish heritage.
Previously, we mapped the gene to a genomic interval of approximately 1 cM on chromosome region 10q23-24, using families from Columbia.

findings.statement: Wang et al. (1999) built a physical map of the UFS critical region on 10q23-q24 and identified new polymorphic markers in it. Haplotype analysis with these markers placed the UFS gene within a single YAC clone of 1,410 kb.
quotes: We established a physical map and identified novel polymorphic markers in the UFS critical region. Haplotype analysis using the new markers mapped the UFS gene within one YAC clone of 1,410 kb.

findings.statement: Wang et al. (1999) found the exact location of the GOT1 gene, which encodes glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase, within the new UFS critical region and determined its genomic structure. Mutation analysis excluded GOT1 as the UFS gene.
quotes: We also determined the precise location of the gene encoding for glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase (GOT1) within the new UFS critical region and determined its genomic structure. However, mutation analysis excluded GOT1 as a candidate for the UFS gene.

findings.statement: Wang et al. (1999) described urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome as a rare autosomal recessive disorder marked by an abnormal facial expression and urinary abnormalities.
quotes: The urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome (UFS) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by abnormal facial expression and urinary abnormalities.

relevance_reason: Maps the urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome gene to 10q23-q24 by homozygosity and linkage-disequilibrium mapping.

findings.statement: Wang et al. (1997) described urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome as a rare autosomal recessive disease characterized by congenital obstructive uropathy and abnormal facial expression; patients present with enuresis, urinary tract infection, hydronephrosis, and voiding dysfunction resulting from neurogenic bladder.
quotes: The urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome (UFS) is a rare autosomal recessive disease characterized by congenital obstructive uropathy and abnormal facial expression.
The patients present with enuresis, urinary-tract infection, hydronephrosis, and voiding dysfunctions as a result of neurogenic bladders.

findings.statement: Wang et al. (1997) performed a genome screen combining homozygosity mapping and DNA pooling in 20 selected UFS patients, one patient pool, and 3 control pools of unaffected relatives; of 36 random markers, D10S677 showed linkage and association with UFS, with a significant excess of homozygosity in patients compared with unaffected relatives (P < 10(-6)) and allele frequency differences between patient and control pools.
quotes: a genome screen using a combination of homozygosity-mapping and DNA-pooling strategies was performed in 20 selected patients, one patient pool, and three control pools (unaffected relatives).

After analyses of 36 randomly chosen markers, D10S677 was identified as being linked to and associated with UFS, as suggested by a significant excess of homozygosity in patients compared with that in unaffected relatives (P < 10(-6))

findings.statement: Wang et al. (1997) fine-mapped the UFS gene with 10 additional markers spanning 22 cM using haplotype (linkage disequilibrium) analysis: all 31 patients were homozygous for D10S1726 and D10S198, about 5 cM telomeric to D10S677, versus only 12% of unaffected relatives (P < 10(-19)). Recombinations in patients heterozygous at flanking markers D10S1433 and D10S603 placed the gene within a 1-cM interval on chromosome 10q23-q24.
quotes: All 31 patients were found to be homozygous for two closely linked markers (D10S1726 and D10S198) located approximately 5 cM telomeric to D10S677, whereas only 12% of the unaffected relatives were homozygous for both markers (P < 10(-19)).
These recombinational events place the UFS gene near D10S1726/D10S198 and within a 1-cM interval defined by D10S1433 and D10S603 on chromosome 10q23-q24.

relevance_reason: The paper describes a large series of patients with urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome, proposes the name for the disorder, and infers autosomal recessive inheritance.

findings.statement: Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) described 36 children, seen between 1965 and 1986, who had enuresis and urinary tract infection together with 'inversion' of facial expression when laughing. Urologic work-up found mild neuropathic bladder in all patients, and most had severe urinary tract damage. About two-thirds of the patients also had moderate to severe constipation.
quotes: Between 1965 and 1986 we saw 36 children with enuresis and urinary tract infection in association with "inversion" of facial expression when laughing.
Urologic work-up of these patients disclosed characteristic findings of mild neuropathic bladder in all cases, with severe urinary tract damage in most of them.
About two thirds of the patients also had moderate to severe constipation.

phenotypes.text: inversion of facial expression when laughing

findings.statement: Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) proposed the name 'urofacial syndrome' for this disorder.
quotes: We suggest the term urofacial syndrome for this disorder.

findings.statement: Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) stated that the clear association between distorted facial expression and neuropathic bladder, which leads to genitourinary tract damage, should prompt urologic evaluation of individuals with 'inversion' of facial expression.
quotes: The clear association of distortion in facial expression and neuropathic bladder with resultant damage to the genitourinary tract should prompt urological evaluation of individuals with "inversion" of facial expression.

findings.statement: Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) concluded that the disorder is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. They based this on its occurrence in multiple sibs, normal parents, increased parental consanguinity, and an equal sex ratio.
quotes: The occurrence of the disorder in multiple sibs, normal parents, increased parental consanguinity, and equal sex ratio indicate autosomal recessive inheritance.

relevance_reason: The title shows this paper is a report on urofacial syndrome, which is this entry's subject. Only the title was supplied, with no abstract or full text, so there is no patient, family, variant or inheritance detail to extract.
Clinical and genetic description of 7 patients from 3 families with Ochoa (urofacial) syndrome; the paper names the syndrome and proposes an inheritance pattern.

findings.statement: Elejalde (1979) described 7 patients (4 females and 3 males) from 3 unrelated families, one of them consanguineous (first cousins), with peculiar facies and gestures while smiling and crying. The patients also had hydronephrosis, hydroureter, intravesical stenosis of the ureter, abnormal caliber of the urethra in the prostatic and membranous portions, urethral valves, and an abnormal trabeculated bladder with diverticula and severe mucosal hypertrophy with sclerotic changes.
quotes: Seven patients (4 females, and 3 males) born in unrelated families, one of them consanguineous (first cousins), were affected by peculiar facies and gestures while smiling and crying, and by hydronephrosis, hydroureter and intravesical stenosis of the ureter

abnormal caliber of the urether in the prostatic and membranous portions, urethral valves, abnormal bladder with trabeculation, and diverticula associated with severe hypertrophy of the mucosa with sclerotic changes

phenotypes.text: peculiar facial expression when smiling and crying

findings.statement: From genetic analysis of the 3 families, Elejalde (1979) concluded that the condition is probably autosomal dominant, with variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance.
quotes: The genetic analysis of these families indicates that the condition is probably autosomal dominant, with variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance.

findings.statement: Elejalde (1979) noted that the peculiar facies allows early recognition of the condition, which could help with early assessment and treatment and perhaps lead to a better prognosis.
quotes: The peculiar facies allows early recognition of the condition, and this can be helpful for early assessment and treatment, leading perhaps to a better prognosis.

findings.statement: Elejalde (1979) called the disorder 'the Ochoa syndrome' and suggested that it represents a change in the facial and urinary developmental fields.
quotes: "The Ochoa syndrome"
The syndrome represents alteration of facial and urinary developmental fields.
